title: Calibrating with a reaction of known delta H

beats.text: There's a second way to calibrate. Instead of a heater, carry out a reaction whose enthalpy change is already known accurately, using a known amount, in the same calorimeter with the same contents.

Here's a hypothetical example. A reference reaction releases fifty point zero kilojoules per mole, and zero point zero four zero zero moles of it react. That releases two point zero zero kilojoules, or two thousand joules. If the temperature rises three point seven zero degrees, the calibration factor is two thousand divided by three point seven zero: about five hundred and forty-one joules per degree.

Electrical calibration is usually preferred, because the energy is measured directly and precisely from the voltage, current and time. A chemical calibration relies on the reference reaction being complete and its enthalpy value being accurate. Either way, calibrate under the same conditions as the experiment you'll use the factor for.
